title: Princess Bamba
hook: another daughter moved to Lahore and kept the family's memory

segments.voice: Yesterday, Princess Sophia at the palace gates, and your line was the princess marched. Did you take a step for a fair cause? Today, her older sister, who went the other way: east. Day nine hundred forty-eight.

A house in Lahore, full of old things. Paintings of men in turbans and jewels. Small portraits on ivory. Pieces of a vanished court, gathered one by one and kept in a city this family once ruled. The woman who gathered them was born in England, raised English, and could have stayed there all her life. Instead she moved to Lahore, the capital her grandfather Ranjit Singh had ruled, and her father had lost as a boy. Today: Princess Bamba.
screen: `A HOUSE FULL OF OLD PORTRAITS.` → `BORN IN ENGLAND.` → `SHE MOVED TO LAHORE.`

segments.voice: First, who she was. Bamba Duleep Singh was Duleep Singh's eldest daughter, Sophia's sister. Like Sophia, she grew up in English houses, far from Punjab, with a father who had been taken from it. Second, the move. She traveled to Punjab, and in the end she stayed. She married a doctor who taught at the medical college in Lahore, and made her home in the old capital. For a child of an exiled family, that was a quiet kind of return: not to a throne, but to a street, a house, a city. Third, the keeping. Over the years she gathered what she could of her family's past: paintings, portraits, objects from Ranjit Singh's court. After she died, the collection she kept passed into the care of the government in Lahore, and today it is known by her name, the Princess Bamba Collection, held at the Lahore Fort. A kingdom was gone. Its rooms had emptied. And one granddaughter set about gathering up what was left. Fourth, the Sikh word nearby. The Gurus use the word simran for remembering: holding the Name of God in mind, again and again, so it isn't lost. What Bamba did is not simran in that sense. Her remembering was of a family and a court. But the two share a shape: memory is not something that simply stays. Somebody keeps it, or it goes. Bamba died in Lahore and is buried there, in the city her family once ruled. That's today's word.
screen: `DULEEP SINGH'S ELDEST DAUGHTER.` · `A QUIET RETURN TO LAHORE.` · `THE PRINCESS BAMBA COLLECTION.` · `MEMORY HAS TO BE KEPT.` · then, large: `SHE KEPT THE MEMORY.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for a family memory. Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind one thing from your family that could easily be lost: a recipe, a saying, a story about a grandparent, a photo in a drawer, a song somebody hummed. Hold it in your mind and look at it closely, the way Bamba might have held a portrait. Who else knows this? If nobody does, it's yours to keep. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Princess Bamba. Bamba Duleep Singh, Duleep's eldest daughter, who made her home in Lahore and gathered her family's past into a collection that bears her name. Today's word.
Your line: she kept the memory. Today, keep one family memory on purpose: write it down, ask about it, or tell it to someone younger. Day nine hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Visitors to the Lahore Fort can see the Princess Bamba Collection of Sikh-era paintings and objects, and some Sikh families keep their own memory of the Sikh kingdom in pictures, stories and visits to Lahore.

notes: Bamba's husband (Dr. David Waters Sutherland) described only as 'a doctor who taught at the medical college in Lahore'; confirm (he is usually described as principal of King Edward Medical College).
How the collection passed to the government after her death (bequest vs. purchase) is told vaguely as 'passed into the care of the government'; confirm.
Her burial place (usually given as the Christian cemetery, Gora Kabristan, in Lahore) is given only as 'buried there'; confirm.
The simran comparison is explicitly distinguished from Bamba's family memory; confirm a Keeper is comfortable with the link. Sukhmani Ang 262 cited for simran; confirm the Ang.
Bamba and Sophia traveled to Punjab together in some accounts; not stated here.
